key_terms.meaning: The three inputs of attention: the query is what you are looking for, each key is the label of a stored item, each value is its content; output = Σᵢ aᵢvᵢ with aᵢ ≥ 0 and Σᵢ aᵢ = 1.
Softmax over the query-key scores, aᵢ = exp(sᵢ)/Σⱼ exp(sⱼ); they say how much of each value is mixed into the output.
Use one query (k = 1) and many image patches as keys and values, so the model pools the patches into one weighted vector instead of a plain average.
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵗ/√dₖ)V, where dₖ is the key vector length; dividing by √dₖ stops the scores from growing large and saturating the softmax.
Q, K and V all come from the same sequence, so every position gathers information from every other position in that sequence.
h attention runs on learned projections of Q, K and V; their outputs are concatenated and mixed by a matrix W₀ so each head can capture a different relation.
A vector added to each token embedding to carry its position, for example sin(pos/10000^(2i/d)) for even i; without it self-attention cannot tell word order.
Hide a fraction of tokens (about 15%) and train the model to predict them from both left and right context; this is BERT's pretraining objective.
Train p(xₜ | x₁, …, xₜ₋₁) at every position using a causal mask so position t cannot see the future; this is GPT's pretraining objective.
Load pretrained weights and keep training on labelled task data with a small learning rate, so the general language knowledge adapts to the specific task.
A stack of causally masked self-attention blocks and feed-forward blocks that outputs a probability for the next token; the shape of GPT-style LLMs.
A measured power law such as L(N) ≈ (N_c/N)^α: test loss falls on a straight line against a log-log plot of parameters N, data tokens D or compute C.
A model trained on human pairwise comparisons that outputs a scalar score r(x, y) for how good answer y is to prompt x.
A term β·KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref) added to the RL objective, where π_ref is the frozen starting model, so the tuned model does not drift away from readable language.
Asking the model to write intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer, which raises accuracy on arithmetic and multi-step questions.
Place a few worked examples of input → output inside the prompt before the real question; the model learns the pattern from context, not from new weights.
A separate, high-priority instruction at the start of a chat that fixes the assistant's role, tone and limits for the whole conversation.
Train a small student model to match the soft output distribution of a large teacher model, keeping much of the teacher's accuracy at lower cost.
Store weights and activations in fewer bits, for example fp32 → int8, which cuts memory about 4× for a small drop in accuracy.
Delete weights, heads or channels with small magnitude and fine-tune the rest, giving a sparse or smaller model that runs faster.

takeaways: Attention is a soft dictionary lookup: compare the query with every key, turn the scores into weights that sum to 1, and return the weighted mix of the values.
Self-attention lets each position of a sequence read every other position, which is why the Transformer replaced recurrence for language tasks.
A Transformer block = multi-head self-attention + residual + layer norm + feed-forward network + residual + layer norm; positional encoding supplies the order.
Pretraining is self-supervised on raw text; fine-tuning reuses those weights for a labelled task, so one pretrained model serves many downstream jobs.
BERT reads both directions with masked prediction and suits understanding tasks; GPT reads left to right with next-token prediction and suits generation.
Scaling laws make training runs plannable: loss falls predictably with parameters, data and compute, so a budget buys a known quality.
RLHF converts human preference comparisons into a reward model and then tunes the language model against it, with a KL penalty holding it near the original.
A prompt is the program for a frozen model; wording, examples and format steer it, and compression (distillation, quantization, pruning) decides where it can be served.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to write the attention equations with Q, K, V, draw the full Transformer block, contrast BERT and GPT objectives, and then connect training, scaling, alignment and deployment of large language models.

bank.q: Explain attention as a soft dictionary lookup. Define query, key and value, write the weight formula, and state why the weights must be normalised.
outline: Query = search request, keys = labels of stored items, values = stored content
Score s(q, kᵢ) for each key, then softmax gives aᵢ ≥ 0, Σaᵢ = 1
Output = Σᵢ aᵢvᵢ, a convex combination of the values
Soft (weighted) vs hard (argmax) lookup — soft keeps the function differentiable
Sharp softmax (low temperature) behaves like nearest-neighbour lookup

bank.q: Describe self-attention and multi-head attention with equations. Why is the dot product divided by √dₖ, and what does each head learn?
outline: Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V from the same sequence X
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵗ/√dₖ)V
Scaling keeps variance of scores near 1 so softmax gradients do not vanish
h heads on d/h-dimension projections, concatenate, multiply by W₀
Different heads attend to syntax, position, coreference, etc.; cost O(n²d)

bank.q: Write the components of a Transformer block and explain the role of positional encoding, residual connections and layer normalisation.
outline: Multi-head self-attention, then add-and-norm, then feed-forward network, then add-and-norm
Residual connections give a short gradient path and let a block learn a small correction
Layer norm normalises across features per token, which stabilises training
Sinusoidal or learned positional vectors added to embeddings; self-attention is permutation-invariant without them
Encoder uses unmasked attention; decoder adds causal mask and cross-attention

bank.q: Compare BERT and GPT: pretraining objective, attention mask, typical use, and the meaning of fine-tuning.
outline: BERT: encoder, bidirectional, masked language modelling plus next-sentence prediction
GPT: decoder, causal mask, next-token prediction on long unlabelled text
BERT suits classification, NER, extractive QA; GPT suits generation, chat, completion
Pretraining is self-supervised, so no human labels are needed
Fine-tuning adds a task head or uses prompt-style output and trains with a small learning rate

bank.q: Define zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting, with one example of each.
outline: Zero-shot: instruction only, no examples
One-shot: one worked example before the question
Few-shot: several examples set the format and label space; this is in-context learning with frozen weights
Chain-of-thought: ask for intermediate steps, then the answer
Examples must match the test format; order and delimiters affect quality

bank.q: For a sequence of three tokens with given 2-dimensional Q, K, V matrices, compute the scaled dot-product attention output step by step and verify the weights sum to 1.
outline: Form S = QKᵗ, list each dot product
Divide by √dₖ with dₖ = 2
Apply softmax row by row and show the sums equal 1
Multiply weights by V and add to get each output vector
Comment on what happens if one score is much larger (weights concentrate)

bank.q: Design a chatbot for a college helpdesk using a frozen language model. Specify the system message, context window policy, retrieval-augmented generation steps and output format control.
outline: System message fixes role, scope, language and refusal policy
Conversation memory trimmed to the context window, oldest turns dropped or summarised
RAG: chunk documents, embed, retrieve top-k by similarity, place text inside delimiters in the prompt
Sampling controls: temperature, top-p, max tokens; JSON or bullet output for the API
Guard against prompt injection by treating retrieved text as data, not instructions

bank.q: A team plans a training run. Explain how scaling laws let them choose parameters N and data tokens D for a fixed compute budget C, and show the FLOPs estimate per token.
outline: Compute C ≈ 6·N·D FLOPs for a dense Transformer (forward plus backward)
Loss falls as a power law in N and in D; each has diminishing returns
Compute-optimal split: grow N and D together, roughly 20 tokens per parameter
Loss also has an irreducible floor; more compute beyond it is wasted
Verify with small runs and extrapolate, then reserve compute for evaluation and fine-tuning

bank.q: A 7-billion-parameter model is served in fp16. Compute the weight memory, then the memory after int8 quantization, and state the expected accuracy and latency effect.
outline: fp16: 2 bytes per parameter, so 7 × 10⁹ × 2 bytes = 14 GB
int8: 1 byte per parameter, so about 7 GB plus small scale factors
Activation memory, KV cache and batch size add to the total
Quantization gives roughly 2× memory saving and faster matrix products
Accuracy loss is small for weight-only 8-bit; check with a validation set

bank.q: Describe the RLHF pipeline end to end. Why is a reward model needed, why is a KL penalty added, and what can go wrong if β is too small or too large?
outline: Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations gives the starting policy π_ref
Humans compare pairs of answers; a reward model is trained with a pairwise ranking loss
RL (for example PPO) maximises E[r(x,y)] − β·KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref)
Small β: reward hacking, verbose or unnatural text, drift from the reference
Large β: model barely changes, alignment gain lost; evaluate with held-out humans

bank.q: For a labelled classification task with limited data, compare full fine-tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning and pure prompting of a large model. Give a recommendation with reasons.
outline: Full fine-tuning: best fit, but one full copy of weights per task and risk of overfitting on small data
Parameter-efficient methods (adapters, low-rank updates): few trainable parameters, many tasks share one base model
Prompting with few-shot examples: no training, fastest to try, weakest on specialised labels
Data size decides: hundreds of labels favour prompting or PEFT; thousands favour full fine-tuning
Also weigh inference cost, latency, privacy and the need to re-train when data changes

bank.q: Explain attention over images with a single query (k = 1). Compare it with global average pooling for image classification and image captioning, and relate it to cross-attention in a caption generator.
outline: CNN or patch encoder gives N region vectors; learned keys and values per region
One query gives N scores, softmax weights, one pooled vector — attention pooling
Global average pooling uses fixed equal weights and cannot select regions
Attention weights are interpretable and can highlight the object
In captioning the decoder query attends over image regions at every step (cross-attention)

bank.q: Compare distillation, quantization and pruning for deploying a language model on a phone. Judge which combination you would use and how you would measure the loss.
outline: Distillation changes the architecture or size; student trained on teacher soft targets
Quantization keeps the architecture and shrinks bits per weight; easiest win, good tooling
Pruning removes weights or heads, needs fine-tuning, gains only with sparse hardware support
Combine: distill to a smaller model, then int8 quantize, then optionally prune
Measure task accuracy, perplexity, latency and memory on the target device, not only on a server

bank.q: A chatbot built on a frozen model starts giving wrong answers after users paste long documents. Analyse the causes using the context window, attention cost and prompt injection, and propose fixes.
outline: Context window is a hard token limit; older turns are silently dropped
Attention cost grows as O(n²) in sequence length; long inputs slow and dilute focus
Middle of a long context is used poorly; key facts lose weight
Retrieved or pasted text can carry instructions — prompt injection; separate data by delimiters and restrict tool access
Fixes: retrieval of top-k chunks, summarise history, pin the system message, cap output with max tokens and top-p

glossary.def: A layer that mixes a set of value vectors using weights computed from the similarity of one query to a set of keys.
The vector that states what the current position or decoder step is looking for.
A vector attached to each stored item, compared with the query to produce a score.
The content vector that is actually averaged, weighted by the attention scores.
softmax(sᵢ) = exp(sᵢ)/Σⱼ exp(sⱼ); it turns arbitrary scores into positive weights that sum to 1.
Attention computed as softmax(QKᵗ/√dₖ)V, the standard attention formula in Transformers.
Attention in which queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence.
Attention where queries come from the decoder and keys and values come from the encoder or image features.
Several attention computations in parallel on projected inputs, concatenated and linearly mixed.
A mask that sets scores to −∞ for future positions so a token can only attend to earlier tokens.
A vector added to token embeddings so the model knows each token's position in the sequence.
Adding a layer's input to its output, x + f(x), which eases gradient flow in deep stacks.
Normalising the features of each token to zero mean and unit variance, then scaling and shifting with learned parameters.
An architecture with an unmasked encoder stack and a masked decoder stack linked by cross-attention, used for translation and captioning.
Self-supervised training on large unlabelled text that produces general-purpose language weights.
Further training of pretrained weights on a smaller labelled dataset for one task.
The maximum number of tokens a model can attend to at once, set by its positional encoding and memory.
The raw, unnormalised score a model produces for each vocabulary token before softmax.
Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose total probability exceeds p, which cuts unlikely tokens.
Improvement in a frozen model's output caused only by examples placed in the prompt.
Fetching relevant documents and placing them in the prompt so the model answers from supplied evidence.
An attack where text inside user data contains instructions that hijack the model away from its system message.
A learned scorer trained on human preference comparisons that RLHF uses as its training signal.
An empirical power-law relation between model loss and parameters, data or compute.
Training a smaller student model to reproduce the output distribution of a larger teacher model.
Representing weights or activations with fewer bits, such as int8 instead of fp32.
